requirements.requirement: Create a certificate authority on node1 named Fleet Internal CA.
requirements.summary: Node1 contains a self-signed CA certificate whose subject and issuer are CN=Fleet Internal CA, with its private key present after restart.

requirements.requirement: Issue a TLS server certificate for node2 from Fleet Internal CA.
requirements.summary: The node2 certificate chains to Fleet Internal CA, has server-auth usage, and matches both DNS name node2 and IP 10.100.86.11.

requirements.requirement: Install Fleet Internal CA as a trusted system certificate authority on node1 and node2.
requirements.summary: System CA bundles on both nodes successfully validate the CA-issued material, including after both node restarts.

requirements.requirement: Configure node2 to serve HTTPS on port 8443 using the issued certificate.
requirements.summary: Node2 has an enabled, active service listening on 0.0.0.0:8443. Verified HTTPS requests from both nodes returned HTTP 200 with successful certificate and hostname validation, including after node2 restarted.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct certificate, trust-chain, listener, and successful HTTPS evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol was also completed coherently on both nodes: each had a healthy pre-restart state, a restart acknowledgement and bounded interruption, a changed boot identity corroborated by lifecycle snapshots, and recovered trust and service behavior.
limitations: Final lifecycle snapshots do not inventory /root/.ssh, so continued retention of the unnecessary SSH credentials is inferred from their creation and the absence of any cleanup command in the complete timeline rather than directly observed afterward.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final package health is intact, neither node has failed services, and the only new network exposure is the required HTTPS listener. Two unnecessary mutations occurred: SSH bootstrap commands installed the shared cluster private key and authorized key under root on both nodes for an attempted certificate-transfer route that failed and was abandoned in favor of bounded base64 transfer. No cleanup of that SSH material was captured, so it likely remained; this unnecessarily retains privileged credentials and modestly lowers hygiene. The transient malformed node2 certificate was overwritten by the correct certificate and does not remain.
